study.title: Job 35 - Elihu, the righteousness of God, and the human cry
study.overview: In this chapter, Elihu corrects the reading he makes of Job's words. He argues that human justice does not increase or diminish God, that the cry of the afflicted often does not turn to the Creator and that the delay of the divine response should not be confused with indifference. The central point is the contrast between the greatness of God and the human tendency to speak without understanding the way He governs and responds.

outline.title: Human justice does not affect God
outline.explanation: Elihu begins by asking whether Job considers it correct to affirm something that, in practice, would put justice itself above that of God. He argues that human sin does not hurt God or his righteousness, and that human righteousness adds nothing to him either. The effect of human conduct lies with other human beings, not on the Lord.

outline.title: The cry of the afflicted and the silence that exposes unbelief
outline.explanation: Elihu describes oppressed people crying out because of the violence of the mighty, but says that many of them do not seek God as Creator. Therefore, their supplications remain empty: not because God is unrighteous, but because they do not address Him with faith and recognition. The problem, according to Elihu, is not a lack of power in God, but arrogance and lack of correct guidance in the cry.

outline.title: The delay of the answer and the word said without knowledge
outline.explanation: Elihu applies this to Job's case: even when God does not seem to act immediately, this does not mean absence of judgment. The chapter ends with the accusation that Job spoke in vain and multiplied words without knowledge, repeating the criticism that his complaints were precipitated and inadequate.

study.context: The chapter is part of Elihu's intervention in Job's book, after Job remained silent before his words. The notes provided show Elihu responding to Job's assertions that, in his reading, sounded as an accusation against the justice and government of God. The scenario is of sapiential debate: poetic discourses in which suffering, justice, divine silence and trust are discussed in the light of Job's experience.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that God does not depend on human virtue and is not harmed by man's sin, even though sin is real and grave. Prayer and the cry must recognize God as Creator and Judge, not just as an appeal for immediate relief. At the same time, the text presents an important pastoral tension: Eliú insists that the delay of God does not prove abandonment, but his words also show the limit of a reading that can reduce Job's suffering the spiritual failure of the sufferer. Theologically, there is here the affirmation of divine transcendence, of human insufficiency to judge the ways of God and the need to speak with reverence before the mystery of providence.

scholarViews.insight: Elihu responds to Job's own argument, but without really adding something new to what others had already said; moreover, he fails to realize that every sin offends God, even though God is not affected as men are.

Elihu accuses Job of saying inappropriate things: first, to treat religion as something useless; then, to imply that God does not listen to the oppressed; finally, to discourage as to the return of divine grace, although the delay does not mean absence of response.

The statement that Job opened his mouth in vain is understood as a warning that the delay of judgment does not prove that God has abandoned him; the delay does not deny the future execution of divine justice.

questions: In what situations can I be talking about God with more confidence than understanding?
When the Lord seems to delay, do I seek God himself or just relief for my pain?
Does my prayer recognize God as Creator and judge, or just as someone who should solve me problems immediately?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to humility. Before turning suffering into accusation against God, pray with honesty and reverence, acknowledging that you may not see all the divine work. At the same time, take seriously the pain of the oppressed and learn to seek it first, rather than just complaining about the circumstances. The concrete practice is to separate a time to reevaluate your recent words about God and replace them with a simple prayer: recognition, request for mercy and trust in the righteousness of the Lord.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are limited and, in some points, present Elihu's reading as if it were the definitive explanation of the book, although Job's own text keeps the discussion open until the divine response. There is also a relevant interpretative observation in Adam Clarke about verse 2, indicating that the phrase may not mean a claim of Job's moral superiority over God; this alternative was preserved as an interpretation, not as absolute certainty. No historical, geographical or linguistic data other than that appears in the notes were used.
